<reason>A more convincingly distinguished English’s value as a shared channel from its role as a gatekeeper for recognition and resources. B established substantial connectivity benefits, but never showed why strengthening local-language scholarship would dismantle that network. Its repeated claim that policy-remediable harms cannot be caused by dominance was unpersuasive. A directly answered the extinction challenge and explained why exclusion and weakened transmission matter before complete destruction. The win remains competitive because A’s overall harm-versus-benefit weighing was qualitative and its concrete evidence of cultural loss limited.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s strongest rebuttal answered “fixable harms versus irreplaceable goods”: original-language scholarship can receive recognition while English translation preserves international reach. This challenged B’s fragmentation counterfactual without denying network benefits. B’s response conflated having the widest audience with needing superior institutional standing.</best_rebuttal>
